An emeritus is a person who has retired from an important professional role — most often at a university or other institution — but has been officially allowed to keep their title as a mark of honor and respect for their years of distinguished service.

Think of it this way: normally, when you leave a job, your title goes with you. You stop being "the director" the day you stop working as the director. But an emeritus is an exception — the institution says, "You've served so well for so long that we want you to carry your title with you for the rest of your life, even though you've stepped down."

So an emeritus is essentially a retired professional who still holds their title — not because they still hold the job, but because the institution decided they earned the right to keep it permanently.
Where you'll most commonly see it

The word is most at home in academia — universities and colleges. A university professor who retires after decades of teaching and research might be designated a Professor Emeritus. In that case, as a noun, we'd call that person simply an emeritus of that university.

But the word travels well beyond academia. You'll also see it used in:

  • Non-profit organizations — a long-serving board chair might be named Chair Emeritus
  • Religious institutions — when Pope Benedict XVI stepped down in 2013, he was referred to as Pope Emeritus
  • Companies and foundations — a retiring CEO or founder might be given the title President Emeritus or Founder Emeritus
  • Academic journals and societies — longtime editors or officers are sometimes given emeritus status

The common thread across all these contexts is the same: retirement + an honorary retention of title.
Why someone becomes an emeritus — and why not everyone does

This status is not automatic upon retirement. It is specifically granted — usually by a vote of the institution's governing body or leadership — to someone who has made an exceptional, long-term contribution.

A junior professor who leaves after three years doesn't become an emeritus. A professor who taught and researched at a university for 35 years, shaped the field, mentored generations of students, and left with a sterling reputation — that person is a strong candidate.

So embedded in the word is an element of distinction and prestige. Calling someone an emeritus is a way of saying: "This person was so valuable that we don't want to sever the connection entirely — we want them to remain part of us, at least in name and spirit."
What an emeritus still does — and doesn't do

This is an important distinction to understand clearly.

What they no longer do:

  • They don't hold the active responsibilities of the role. An emeritus professor doesn't have a required teaching load, isn't obligated to sit on committees, and doesn't draw a full salary for those duties.
  • They don't have formal authority in the way active office-holders do.

What they often still do (voluntarily):

  • Many emeriti (the plural — more on that below) continue to attend institutional events, give occasional lectures, or speak at conferences.
  • Some continue doing research and writing on their own terms, at their own pace.
  • They often serve as mentors and advisors to younger colleagues or students, drawing on their deep experience.
  • Some teach an occasional course if they wish, though it is usually not required.

The key word is voluntarily. An emeritus is free from the obligations of the role but often still contributes because of genuine passion and continued connection to their field. The title gives them a dignified, ongoing identity within the institution without the pressures of full-time employment.

Plural: The plural of emeritus is emeriti (pronounced as three syllables: eh-MER-ih-tie, though you said no pronunciation — just noting it for your awareness). So you might read: "The university invited all its emeriti to the reunion."

In informal or everyday writing, you'll also sometimes see emerituses as a plural, though emeriti is the more traditional and widely respected form.

Feminine form: Technically, the feminine singular is emerita, and the feminine plural is emeritae. So a retired female professor might be called Professor Emerita. However, in modern usage — especially in informal American English — emeritus and emeriti are increasingly used regardless of gender, and many institutions apply them universally. You may encounter both approaches, and neither is considered wrong in contemporary usage.
What emeritus does NOT mean — clearing up possible confusion

It does not mean the person was pushed out or forced to retire. Quite the opposite — emeritus status is typically associated with a graceful, honored exit. It implies the person left on good terms and with the institution's deep gratitude.

It does not mean the person is still actively doing the job. The retirement is real. The title is honorary. Confusing the two is a common mistake.

It does not imply the person is no longer active or sharp. Many emeriti are prolific contributors to their fields long after retirement. The title says nothing about their current energy or intellectual activity — only about their formal employment status.

It is not the same as "honorary." An honorary degree or title (like an honorary doctorate) is given to someone who was never formally part of the institution — often to recognize an outsider's achievements. An emeritus title, by contrast, is given to someone who was very much inside the institution — who actually held the role — and is now retired from it.
A few example sentences to anchor the meaning

• "After forty years of teaching literature, Professor Nakamura retired and became an emeritus of the university." — She no longer teaches full-time but retains the professor title.
  • "The foundation's emeriti were invited to address the new board members." — Retired past leaders who hold honorary titles were brought in to share wisdom.
  • "As an emeritus, he was still seen regularly in the library, working on his research." — Retired, but still voluntarily engaged in his scholarly work.
  • "She was named emerita of the institute, the first woman to receive that honor." — A distinguished retired female member, given the feminine form of the title.

If you ever need to recall this word in one sentence: An emeritus is a retired professional — especially from academia or a prestigious institution — who has been officially allowed to keep their title for life as an honor for outstanding, long-term service.
